enc.title: Examiner's favourites: diffraction and Bloch waves

source.file: materials/solid-state/old-exams (oral protocols HS04, HS05, HS06, HS10, HS11, HS13, HS14, HS15, FS05)
source.where: questions the examiners asked repeatedly, rewritten as written multiple choice; answers our own

questions.q: Why do X-ray Bragg peaks of a crystal have different heights?
options: Structure factor (basis), atomic form factor (falls with $|\mathbf G|$) and the Debye-Waller factor
Only because of the detector angle
All allowed peaks are equally high
Because of the photon energy only
questions.explain: $I\propto|F_{hkl}|^2$ with $F=\sum_jf_j(\mathbf G)e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r_j}$; $f_j$ decreases with $|\mathbf G|$, and thermal vibrations multiply by $e^{-\langle u^2\rangle G^2/3}$. (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: How does the height of a Bragg peak change when the crystal is heated?
options: It decreases (Debye-Waller factor), most for large $|\mathbf G|$; the width stays sharp
The peak broadens and disappears at once
questions.explain: $e^{-\langle u^2\rangle G^2/3}$ with $\langle u^2\rangle\propto T$ at high $T$; the intensity goes into a diffuse background. (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: Thermal neutrons (energy $\approx25$ meV) are ideal to measure
options: phonon dispersions by inelastic scattering: their energy is comparable to phonon energies
questions.explain: Moderated to room temperature, $k_BT\approx25$ meV and $\lambda\approx1.8$ Å: both energy and wavelength match phonons. (asked in: HS05)

questions.q: Is a Bloch function $\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)$ periodic in the lattice?
options: No, only $u_{\mathbf k}$ and $|\psi_{\mathbf k}|^2$ are
Yes, but only for free electrons
questions.explain: $\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)$: periodic only up to a phase (truly periodic at $\mathbf k=0$ or $\mathbf k$ a reciprocal lattice vector). (asked in: HS14)

source.file: materials/solid-state/old-exams (oral protocols HS04, HS05, HS06, HS10, HS11, HS13, HS14, HS15, FS05)
source.where: questions the examiners asked repeatedly, rewritten as written multiple choice; answers our own

questions.q: Why is the phonon density of states $\propto\omega^2$ in the Debye model?
options: Linear dispersion $\omega=v_sk$ in 3D: number of modes $\propto k^3\propto\omega^3$
questions.explain: $D(\omega)=\frac{3V\omega^2}{2\pi^2v_s^3}$ up to $\omega_D$, fixed by the total $3N$ modes. The real DOS has van Hove singularities and is not $\propto\omega^2$ everywhere; Einstein uses a $\delta$-peak. (asked in: HS04, HS10, HS14)

questions.q: Which has the higher Debye temperature, diamond or lead?
options: Diamond ($\approx2200$ K vs $\approx100$ K): light atoms and stiff bonds
It depends only on the lattice type
questions.explain: $\omega\sim\sqrt{C/M}$: small $M$ and large spring constant give high frequencies (Kittel: C 2230 K, Pb 105 K). (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: Why do the Debye and Einstein models agree with Dulong-Petit at high $T$?
options: Each atom is 3 classical oscillators: $6$ quadratic degrees of freedom $\times\frac12k_BT$ gives $3k_B$ per atom
questions.explain: Equipartition holds once $k_BT\gg\hbar\omega$ for all modes. (asked in: HS10, HS14)

questions.q: Why does the Einstein model fail at low temperatures?
options: It predicts an exponential decrease of $C_V$; experiment shows $T^3$ from the low-energy acoustic phonons it ignores
questions.explain: All modes at one frequency $\omega_E$ freeze out together; long-wavelength acoustic modes always remain excitable. (asked in: HS15)

questions.q: Why is diamond an excellent heat conductor although it is an insulator?
options: Phonons carry the heat, and with its high $\Theta_D$ few umklapp phonons exist at room temperature: long phonon mean free path
questions.explain: $\kappa=\frac13Cv\ell$; umklapp scattering $\propto e^{-\Theta_D/bT}$ is weak when $\Theta_D\gg T$. (asked in: HS06)

questions.q: In an optical phonon of a diatomic chain at $k=0$, neighbouring atoms
options: move against each other (centre of mass of the cell at rest)
move only if they are of the same mass
questions.explain: $\omega=\sqrt{2C(1/M_1+1/M_2)}$ at $k=0$; at the zone boundary only one sublattice moves in each branch. (asked in: HS10, test exam HS26)

source.file: materials/solid-state/old-exams (oral protocols HS04, HS05, HS06, HS10, HS11, HS13, HS14, HS15, FS05)
source.where: questions the examiners asked repeatedly, rewritten as written multiple choice; answers our own

questions.q: Order of magnitude: $E_F$ of a typical metal versus $k_BT$ at room temperature?
questions.explain: $T_F\sim10^4$-$10^5$ K $\gg300$ K: the electron gas is highly degenerate. (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: Why is the electronic heat capacity of a metal $\propto T$ and so small?
options: Only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $E_F$ can be excited (Pauli): $C_e=\frac{\pi^2}2Nk_B\frac T{T_F}$
questions.explain: Fraction $T/T_F$ of the electrons, each with energy $\sim k_BT$. At low $T$ it beats the phonon $T^3$: plot $C/T$ vs $T^2$. (asked in: HS11, HS15)

questions.q: Why may electron-electron scattering usually be neglected in a metal?
options: Pauli blocking: few final states are free (rate $\propto(T/T_F)^2$), and the Coulomb interaction is screened
questions.explain: Both partners must end in empty states near $E_F$: phase space $\propto(k_BT)^2$. (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: Is the 3D free-electron density of states mass dependent?
questions.explain: Heavier carriers mean a flatter $E(k)$ and more states per energy (in 2D it is mass dependent but energy independent). (asked in: HS14)

source.file: materials/solid-state/old-exams (oral protocols HS04, HS05, HS06, HS10, HS11, HS13, HS14, HS15, FS05)
source.where: questions the examiners asked repeatedly, rewritten as written multiple choice; answers our own

questions.q: An electric field is switched on, then off. How does the shifted Fermi sphere return to equilibrium?
options: Through scattering on phonons and impurities with relaxation time $\tau$; only electrons near the Fermi surface scatter
questions.explain: The displacement $\delta k=eE\tau/\hbar$ is tiny compared to $k_F$; scattering moves electrons from the front to the back of the sphere. (asked in: FS05, HS14, HS15)

questions.q: Why does the resistivity of a metal grow linearly with $T$ above $\Theta_D$?
options: The number of phonons (scatterers) grows $\propto T$ ($n_B\approx k_BT/\hbar\omega$)
questions.explain: $\rho=m/(ne^2\tau)$ with $1/\tau\propto$ number of phonons; $n$ and $v_F$ are $T$-independent in a metal. Below $\Theta_D$: $\rho\propto T^5$ (fewer phonons $\propto T^3$, small-angle scattering $\propto T^2$), then the residual value from impurities. (asked in: HS13, HS15)

questions.q: Why does copper conduct much better than stainless steel?
options: The alloy is disordered: strong scattering on the random atoms gives a large residual resistivity (Matthiessen)
Copper has more electrons per atom
questions.explain: $\rho=\rho_{\rm ph}(T)+\rho_{\rm imp}$; in an alloy $\rho_{\rm imp}$ dominates even at room temperature. (asked in: HS06)

questions.q: Which difference between metal and semiconductor makes their $\rho(T)$ opposite?
options: In the semiconductor $n(T)$ grows exponentially; in the metal $n$ is fixed and only $\tau$ falls with $T$
questions.explain: $\sigma=ne\mu$: for semiconductors the activated $n(T)$ wins over the mobility. (asked in: HS13)

questions.q: Why is there a factor 2 in $n_i\propto T^{3/2}e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$?
options: $np\propto e^{-E_g/k_BT}$ and $n=p$, so $n=\sqrt{np}$: $E_F$ sits near mid-gap
Because of the two spin states
It is a typo, it should be $E_g/k_BT$
questions.explain: Law of mass action; each carrier only needs $E_g/2$ measured from $E_F$. (asked in: HS13, HS15)

questions.q: $\ln n$ vs $1/T$ of an n-doped semiconductor shows (from low to high $T$)
questions.explain: At room temperature a typical doped Si is in saturation. (asked in: HS06, HS13)

questions.q: Why is the donor ionisation energy so small ($\sim10$-$50$ meV) compared to hydrogen ($13.6$ eV)?
options: Hydrogen model with $m^*$ and screening $\varepsilon_r$: $E_d=13.6\,{\rm eV}\cdot\frac{m^*/m}{\varepsilon_r^2}$
Because the donor is a heavy atom
questions.explain: Si: $\varepsilon_r\approx12$, so the orbit is large (many lattice constants) and weakly bound. (asked in: HS06, HS13)

questions.q: With higher doping $N_D$ the Fermi level of an n-type semiconductor (saturation regime)
options: moves closer to the conduction band edge
questions.explain: $n=N_D=N_{\rm eff}e^{-(E_C-E_F)/k_BT}$. (asked in: HS13, HS14)

questions.q: Higher doping on both sides of a pn junction makes the depletion zone
questions.explain: More fixed charge per volume is needed to drop the same diffusion voltage. (asked in: HS04, HS13, HS14)

questions.q: How can the reverse (saturation) current of a diode be reduced?
options: Use a larger-gap material (Si rather than Ge) or cool it: $I_s\propto n_i^2\propto e^{-E_g/k_BT}$
questions.explain: $I=I_s(e^{eU/k_BT}-1)$; minority carriers are thermally generated. (asked in: HS05, HS13)

questions.q: Can the diffusion voltage $eU_D$ of a (non-degenerate) pn junction exceed the band gap?
options: No: it is the difference of the two Fermi levels, both inside the gap
questions.explain: $eU_D=E_g-(E_C-E_F)_n-(E_F-E_V)_p(asked in: HS14)

questions.q: What causes ferromagnetism in Fe?
options: Exchange interaction (Pauli principle + Coulomb), not the magnetic dipole interaction
questions.explain: Dipolar energies are $\sim1$ K, far too weak for $T_C\approx1000$ K. (asked in: HS04, HS06)

questions.q: Why are Fe, Co, Ni ferromagnets but Pd and Pt not?
options: Stoner: $I\,D(E_F)>1$; the narrow d bands give a high $D(E_F)$, and in Pd/Pt it is just too small
Pd and Pt have no d electrons
questions.explain: Pd is a nearly-ferromagnetic, strongly enhanced Pauli paramagnet. (asked in: HS06)

questions.q: Pauli paramagnetism of conduction electrons is
questions.explain: Only electrons near $E_F$ can flip. Landau diamagnetism of free electrons is $-\frac13\chi_P$. (asked in: HS13, HS14)

questions.q: Is the magnetic moment of the electron parallel to its spin?
questions.explain: Same for the orbital moment. (asked in: FS05, HS13)

questions.q: Larmor diamagnetism of closed shells is largest for
options: big atoms (large $Z\langle r^2\rangle$): go down the periodic table
it is the same for all atoms
questions.explain: $\chi\propto-Z\langle r^2\rangle$. (asked in: HS14)

questions.q: Why does $M$ not vanish at $B=0$ on a hysteresis loop?
options: Domain walls are pinned at defects; the domain configuration depends on history (remanence)
Because the exchange is switched off
questions.explain: A reverse coercive field is needed to move the walls. (asked in: HS04)
